Snorting
SNOR-ting
n. (the blowing of warhorses; the sound of the invasion heard from Dan)
Imitative, from Middle English snorten. At Jeremiah 8:16 it renders Hebrew nachrah, a snorting, from a root meaning to blow through the nostrils — used once in Scripture.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah reports the invasion first as a noise: The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land, and all that is in it; the city, and those that dwell therein. Dan was the northern limit of the land, the top of the phrase from Dan to Beersheba, so the sound is at the border and has not yet arrived. The whole land trembles at a noise. Anyone who has heard cavalry at close quarters will recognize the detail: the snort of a warhorse before the charge is a sound designed by nature to unnerve.

Job, in the LORD's speech out of the whirlwind, gives the same animal a whole paragraph and one unforgettable line: Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? the glory of his nostrils is terrible. The horse in Scripture is almost always a military animal, and the Bible's attitude toward it is consistent and unfashionable: the horse is magnificent, and trusting it is folly. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God. Jeremiah's snorting is the sound of a power Judah could not answer, and the chapter's own explanation of why it is coming has nothing to do with cavalry: they had healed the hurt of the daughter of the people slightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there was no peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the forcing of air with violence through the nose, as a horse; the sound so made.

expand to see more

SNORTING, n. The act of forcing the air violently through the nose; the sound made by a horse.

SNORT, v.i. To force the air with violence through the nose, so as to make a noise, as high spirited horses.

NEIGH, v.i. To utter the voice of a horse, called whinnying.

CAVALRY, n. A body of military troops on horses; a division of an army serving on horseback.

TREMBLE, v.i. To shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold or weakness; to quake; to quiver.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 8:16 — "The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land, and all that is in it; the city, and those that dwell therein."

Jeremiah 8:17 — "For, behold, I will send serpents, cockatrices, among you, which will not be charmed, and they shall bite you, saith the LORD."

Job 39:20 — "Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? the glory of his nostrils is terrible."

Psalm 20:7 — "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."

Modern Corruption

Military and technological strength is trusted as though it were the decisive factor, which is exactly the confidence Scripture names as folly while never denying that the horses are terrible.

expand to see more

The Bible is not naive about force. Job's warhorse paragraph is one of the great pieces of writing on the animal in any language, and Jeremiah reports that a whole nation trembled at a noise from the border. What Scripture denies is that force is where safety comes from. An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength. Israel's kings were forbidden to multiply horses to themselves, and Solomon broke the rule first and largest. The prohibition was not a dislike of cavalry; it was a fence against the confidence cavalry produces.

Jeremiah 8 makes the real cause of the disaster explicit, and it is not a shortfall in defence. The chapter is full of the failure of the men who should have spoken: they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there was no peace. A nation is not destroyed because the enemy's horses are loud. It is destroyed because the watchmen said everything was fine. The application is closer to home than the cavalry: where preaching has gone soft, the snorting at the border is already a mercy, because it is the last warning anyone is going to get.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nachrah (H5170), a snorting; abbir (H47), a strong one, a stallion; sus (H5483), a horse.

expand to see more

Hebrew nachrah (H5170) — a snorting; used once, of the horses heard from Dan.

Hebrew abbir (H47) — mighty, strong; here the stallions whose neighing shook the land.

Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; almost always a war animal in Scripture.

Hebrew tsiphoni (H6848) — a cockatrice or adder; the serpents of the next verse, which will not be charmed.

Hebrew ra'ash (H7493) — to quake; the trembling of the whole land at a sound.

Usage

"“The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan” — the invasion arrives first as a noise."

"“the glory of his nostrils is terrible” — the LORD's own description of the animal."

"“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” — and where the trembling ought to stop."
